We have been instructed that due to our lack of a DVA, for an aircraft on an IFR missed approach we may only tell the aircraft to execute the published missed approach, which is for the aircraft to turn 180 degrees and start climbing, which will obviously place the aircraft on a collision course with anyone behind it. For an aircraft on a visual approach, we must tell the aircraft to remain in the pattern and re-sequence it ourselves, no matter how far we have to take it outside of our airspace to do so (VNY is five miles west of BUR and WHP is five miles northwest of BUR. Both are busy Class D airports and keeping a jet in the pattern after a go-around at BUR often results in violating the airspace of one of these airports and losing any positive separation with aircraft in the Class D airspace).I have been filing reports for the past year about how unsafe the missed approach situation is at BUR. The standard when we have a go-around is for LC to call SCT and find a 'Work-around' since the only thing we're allowed to assign (the published missed) results in the aircraft being placed in direct conflict with any aircraft behind it. The old procedure was to give the missed approach aircraft the SID heading and altitude (heading 210 and 4,000) to turn the aircraft into a 'Departure' to be shipped back to TRACON and sequenced. This is what SCT usually asks us to do on a missed approach, but we're not allowed to do it. In this case, the SCT controller asked for the aircraft on a 210 heading and climbing to 4,000 and the controller at LC issued it. The plane was shipped back to SCT and sequenced.When Aircraft X came back from approach for his second attempt at landing, he got an RA over VNY again and had to go around again. This time LC didn't have time to call SCT and try to find a 'Work-around;' and issued the aircraft the published missed approach procedure, which is what we've been instructed we must do. Aircraft X commenced with the published missed approach procedure and immediately lost separation with Aircraft Y, an IFR who was off VNY. At their closest, the aircraft were at 1.3 miles and around 500 feet of separation, but there was never a time when any form of positive separation existed between the two.I have been reporting this situation for over a year. In all my years controlling I have never seen a situation as unsafe as the current missed approach procedure at BUR. We have been told that we must place planes in an unsafe situation, as the only thing we can do on a go-around is issue the published missed approach, which causes the plane to turn 180 degrees and start climbing, which will put him into the face of anyone on approach behind him or anyone on a SID off VNY. We have been told that the solution is to ship the aircraft to SCT as soon as possible so that they can fix the problem. That is ridiculous. I have never, ever heard of anywhere that has a procedure that equates to 'Point two planes at each other, allow an unsafe situation to develop, and then let someone else take care of it.' The old procedure was for us to give the missed approach plane the SID heading and altitude. That was taken away about a year and a half ago because it was determined to be illegal since we don't have a DVA at BUR. We have been told that getting us a DVA [Diverse Vector Areas] is a 'High priority;' but it's been over a year and a half now. If getting us a DVA is what it will take so that we can actually control aircraft and keep them from losing separation, then get us a DVA and get it to us now. As of now, we don't have the tools we need to keep the airplanes apart at BUR. This will not be the last time there is a loss of separation due to this situation.
1237573: On approach to Reno [Runway] 16R, encountered moderate turbulence, LLWS, shifting high winds with severe gusts and blowing dust. Airspeed fluctuations on final with a shift to a tailwind necessitated a missed approach go around. While accomplishing the missed approach encountered strong moderate turbulence at flaps 3 and the gear up, atmospheric conditions created an airspeed gain in excess of 30 to 45 knots thus overspeeding the flaps for configuration. The pitch was immediately adjusted but the overspeed occurred with a massive airspeed gain. In reconfiguring to flaps one, a similar airspeed gain caused a second overspeed in the flaps one configuration. The pitch attitude was adjusted and no further over speeds occurred. Upon taxi to gate, overspeed condition was written up and reported to maintenance for inspection. The winds were changing constantly gusting to 35/50 knots. The First Officer configured early to get the plane stabilized. At approx. 1,000 feet we were losing airspeed and altitude and showing a 15 knot tailwind while tower was still calling a 30 knot headwind. I could also see a dust line coming down the runway towards the landing zone. I directed a go around and while climbing we got the 30-40 knot headwind gusts. While getting the flaps from 3 to 1, the airspeed hit the bottom of the red line twice. The moderate turbulence and gusts made it difficult to read the speed tape and fly the plane. After landing on the second attempt, I called Maintenance Control and wrote up the flap overspeed.
1237585: Arrived at aircraft and discovered maintenance working on a L3 window overheat written up by previous crew. As mechanic removed the RAM mount [iPad holder] from L3 window, I noticed the window was delaminated where the ram mount had been stuck to the window. I wrote up the delamination. Both issues were deferred. No attention was brought to the fact the RAM mount had been stuck on that window. I am concerned the black rubber suction cups we are sticking on the heated window are absorbing heat from both the window heat and sun then reflecting the heat back into the window. I removed a RAM mount from the window on the next plane we flew and discovered the window was hot where the mount had been placed. I am concerned the potential damage caused by this excessive heat could be a serious safety issue and also concerned we may be incurring unnecessary and significant maintenance costs.
1237599: Cruising at FL240 on the Ivane5. ATC cleared us to descend via the IVANE RNAV STAR. Looked at the next fix Mayos, and there was not a restriction set in the FMS. Set 6,000 Ft in altitude alert window. Began to pick up a little chop, and I said to First Officer (FO): I think I'll take the descent now. Engaged managed descent, trusting the FMS, and FO said 'I'll let him know.' So he called ATC out of FL240, and he said, 'You have to cross Mayos at FL240.' He then asked if we could get cleared down to FL220, and ATC granted this request with descend to FL220 and then descend via the Ivane5.' We had started down, but were about 200 Ft below FL240, or 23,800 Ft when we intervened and leveled off.Because we were at a lower cruising altitude, FL240, I think that the FMS didn't accurately sense a crossing restriction at the next intersection on the arrival, and therefore ACCEPTED my input of a managed descent. There was not a window altitude at Mayos this time. This would have been contrary to the star which requires us to cross Mayos between FL260 and FL240. Certainly updating the software to retain crossing restrictions, and to honor them in managed descent would be nice, regardless if already at cruising altitude. Now I must check the arrival's Jepp page when initially beginning a descent, and then continuously check it during a descent against the glass. I remember when I first came over to the airbus from the 737, and the check airman said, 'The glass never lies.' In this case, I'm finding out more and more, that the glass does indeed lie.
1237619: Approach control cleared us for the approach (Rwy 27L), caution wake turbulence following a Boeing 757, maintain 180 knots until TAFFS, contact tower control at TAFFS. We then switched the frequency to tower, and continued the approach. Tower called us prior to TAFFS and told us to go back to approach control. We returned to approach control and he told us to slow to 170 knots until TAFFS and we should have stayed with him till we got closer to TAFFS so we would have heard him when he wanted us to slow an additional 10 knots. If Pilots are told to contact tower and call at a certain fix inbound, then we have to switch frequency at some point. The approach controller assumed I would stay with him longer than I did. However, when he called for us we were no longer with him, because he did not ask for us to stay with him. As the pilot flying during a visual approach I was 'heads up' and did not notice that the captain immediately switched to tower from the approach frequency. Moments later, tower transmitted a call to us asking if we were on and asking us to switch back to approach control. Chicago approach when contacted had a 10 knot speed change and explained the significance of the phrase 'contact tower at...'No significant aircraft separation was an issue, as the speed change seemed to be for wake turbulence reasons, and no further communications about the incident came from approach or tower, other than approach grumbling something about '...the third one today...'In a debrief of the incident the captain said he has always switched immediately to tower when given that instruction, and we discussed what Chicago approach expects him to do.In our debrief we discussed the fact that Chicago is one of a very few places that uses that procedure for transferring to tower. Also we discussed that depending on the weather conditions the approach controller will give 2 different clearances:'..contact tower at...' meaning stay on approach and switch to tower at the OM.'...contact tower now...' which when complied with TOWER will acknowledge and then say 'report at...' OM.The different clearances depending on weather conditions for this specific airport lead to an expectation bias on the part of the captain. As the pilot flying I should have been monitoring the radio selection.
1237636: On takeoff out of IAH Rwy 27, ATC gave us a turn at 1500 FT to the north. I saw the pilot not flying (PNF) move his hand towards the flap handle. And the after TKOF checklist was completed. On descent for the approach I called for flaps 9 and the PNF went to move the flap handle and realized that it was already set at flaps 9, he asked if I had moved the handle and my response was no. That was when we realized we just flew the flight at flaps 9. Our speed in the climb and cruise never went above 280 KIAS. When we landed, I called Maintenance control and told them what had happened and entered in the logbook. They called our local Maintenance and they came up to the plane at the gate and inspected it and signed the aircraft off. Unusual TKOF in IAH RWY 27 with a turn to the north at a specified height at 1500 FT which we were climbing through which interrupted the flow. Need to verify the flaps at 0, even when interrupted by ATC. Be better at verifying the checklist has been completed with what is exactly on the checklist. On approach, the Captain (CA) called for 'Flaps 9.' I placed my hand on the lever and noticed it already said 9 on the EICAS. I asked if he had moved it, he replied 'No.' That's when it dawned on us that we flew the entire flight at flaps 9. Reflecting on the flight, everything was normal leading up to the takeoff. On the initial climb, I made the Flap Retraction Altitude call. The CA called for 'FLC, Flaps 0, set climb, after takeoff check.' As I placed my hand on the flap lever Tower said 'out of one thousand five hundred, turn right heading 350. Say altitude.' I was caught off guard by the call as we had already passed 1,500. I double checked the altitude and responded with '1600.' I assume at this moment I moved my left hand off the flap lever and turned the heading bug. I continued with the rest of the after takeoff flow and accomplished the checklist, reading aloud 'Flaps indicating 0.' I remember doing this but do not remember if the EICAS indicated 9 or 0. We were restricted to 270 KIAS in the climb, and Smart CI recommended approximately 270 for cruise. I believe the max speed we encountered on the descent was 280 KIAS. After landing we called MX, who inspected the flaps and signed the aircraft off.-somewhat unusual departure from Rwy 27, with a turn to the north-unanticipated clearance to turn after 1500, which interrupted the after takeoff flow-complacency with the after takeoff checklist item 'Flaps indicating 0'-Failure to retract flaps-Failure to trap the error with the checklistI have increased vigilance on all checklist items, specifically 'Flaps indicating 0' on the after takeoff check. The company has already made this a focus area with the only verbal call on the silent after takeoff check.
1237645: Key West was reporting IMC and conducting ASR to [RWY] 27. There is not a DA (Decision Altitude) listed under the night section and the notes are implied to circle to land, which we were not doing. We held and contacted the dispatcher to get clarification. They concluded that I was legal to commence the approach if the tower is currently conducting it and can relay the DA and missed approach instructions. The tower was able to give me all the information and clarified they are doing ASR [RWY] 27 approaches at night. We continued based on the information given to us and broke out of IMC conditions, called it visual at 1,300 MSL and landed. Received a call from flight to EYW, stating that weather was no longer VFR and was sitting at 900 ft., 10 sm. He wanted clarity on whether or not he would be able to shoot an ASR approach on runway 27 under those flight conditions since the ASR's minimums were published as 500 ft. and 1/1/4 SM but had an N/A in a column referencing 'Night Flying.' While I reviewed the WX, I asked another Dispatcher, if he could call ATC and verify that they do conduct ASR approaches at night in EYW. He called and spoke with Both MIA Center and the EYW TOWER, and they both confirmed that they do conduct night time ASR approaches into EYW and would be able to take care of the flight. After getting confirmation from both ATC and the Tower, I felt reassured and I relayed this information to the Captain then told him to contact the tower if he needed further confirmation but that they had told us that they could accommodate him with an ASR approach. The Duty Manager was present for the event and also agreed with the decision since both MIA ATC and the EYW Tower said they did conduct night time ASR approaches but after we all thought it over we thought it best to try to get a hold of the DO (Director of Operations), and get his final opinion on the flight. While the other Dispatcher called the DO, I tried multiple times to reach the flight to ask him to have ATC put him into a holding pattern but had no luck. After speaking with the DO, the other Dispatcher said the DO told him not to have the flight land even though we got confirmation from both MIA ATC and the EYW tower because it goes against the approach plate and they should have never allowed the flight to do the ASR approach to begin with. I notified the other Dispatcher that I was unable to reach the flight and he called the tower to have them put the flight into holding, but they had informed him that the flight had just landed. To avoid this happening in the future if the approach plate seems confusing I will not make a decision until I have properly used all my resources. If there should be a next time, I will take the approach plate at face value and not base it solely off of interpretation as well as consult with the supervisor or DO.
1237652: In VMC at 4,500 MSL we encountered sustained moderate turbulence. During this time, we encountered an isolated incidence of severe turbulence, resulting in momentary loss of control, an altitude loss of approximately 200 feet, and the pilot and copilot striking their heads on the ceiling. There were no passengers on board. We were approximately 75 miles northeast of BIL.
1237662: We were assigned 4R at BOS at night, about 6 miles out we were assigned 4L. I told the FO unable. He accepted the clearance from ATC. I told him again that I wanted to continue with 4R. He was unable to relay this as the frequency was congested. ATC then gave us a heading in the direction of 4L, by now it was late to inform ATC. I lined up with 4L runway and proceeded uneventfully through landing. So I thought, until today when Flight Operations Quality Assurance called and said we had a flap overspeed. I believe we did not notice this due to the multiple distractions from the late runway switch. On landing I advised the copilot not to accept any runway clearances without checking with the Captain. He agreed. ATC should not change runways so close in, nor should pilots accept these changes so close in. Causes distractions.
1237679: ATC gave us conflicting clearances for the arrival (3 times), so we were high coming into the approach phase. I had the speed brake deployed and had pulled the throttles back to try to come down to glideslope. The aircraft started to level off while we were high and I went to VS (Vertical Speed) and put in 1,800 feet rate of descent, the aircraft came out of VS and started to level again causing the aircraft to slow. The FO called we [are] in the hook (minimum maneuver speed) and I started to add power, we had a stick shaker for about 1 second. We caught the error and corrected it. We made a stable approach and landed without any further problems. Too many changes too close to the airport. I think the system worked as we caught our error and corrected it in a timely manner. During the arrival into San Jose, Costa Rica, ATC gave us conflicting clearances for the arrival (3 times), which caused us to be high on PATH. The last altitude assigned was 9,000 feet (I think). The PF deployed the speed brakes in an effort to regain the PATH. The last clearance given was to proceed to ALTOS and descend via the PARRITA 4 arrival. I reprogrammed the FMS for the current clearance. The PF noticed that we were still high on path and reverted the vertical mode to VS (Vertical Speed), selecting -1800 FPM... the aircraft began to transition to a -1800 rate of descent, however we began to slow below our current flap maneuver speed. (I believe we were flaps 1 and there was a speed restriction at TOMAS of 160). The MCP altitude was not set to a lower altitude and the aircraft began to level and slow. I announced that we were in the hook (minimum maneuver speed). The PF began to add power, however stick shaker activated briefly. The PF noticed that the VS window closed (because we captured the MCP altitude). I stated that we did not have the lower altitude set. The PF set the lower altitude in the MCP and selected Flight Level Change (I think). A good correction was made to return above maneuver speed for the current flap setting. The remainder of the arrival an approach was stable and without incident. Due to the language challenges in Costa Rica and the conflicting ATC clearances, there was a breakdown in CRM. While attempting to program the FMS for the current clearance, I (PM) did not verify the correct lower altitude was set in the MCP. Additionally, the PF did not set a lower altitude in the MCP, reverted to VS to try to regain PATH, did not recognize the speed reduction, and did not quickly recognize that the plane was leveling at the current MCP altitude. As a crew, we could have been better at implementing the FOM automation philosophy. Once we noticed that we deviated from our flap maneuver speed, less time should have been spent trying to correctly automate.
